<reason>Side B built the stronger path to victory by articulating a concrete enforcement mechanism—ex-ante constraints via automatic expiry, notification requirements, and retrospective justification—that neutralizes A's "72-hour tribunal" critique. B successfully reframed the debate from whether rules can stop existential crises (where A is strong) to whether they can discipline the more common pre-emptive and prolonged bans that create regional cascades. In Rebuttal 2, B exposed a fatal gap in A's position: A admitted to accepting limits on bans but rejected all enforceable mechanisms, leaving only voluntary solidarity and domestic accountability, which B persuasively argued externalize hunger to neighbors who cannot vote. While A's sovereignty and crisis-management case was vivid and plausible, it remained defensive against B's more complete causal framework addressing the collective action problem.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (A1/A2) was decisive: it directly answered A's pressure questions by explaining that pre-commitment mechanisms (sunset clauses, ceilings on renewal) operate before any ruling, while exposing A's admission that they support limits in principle but reject the only enforceable mechanism proposed, effectively conceding that their alternative relies on tools that "disappear first" in crises.</best_rebuttal>
